Grief is emotional, but it is also a whole-body stress response, so sleep disruption, poor appetite, anxiety, palpitations and concentration problems can be genuine physical effects of mourning rather than “just imagination.” Acute bereavement can increase stress hormones, heart rate, blood pressure and blood-clotting tendency, while disrupted sleep, eating and medication-taking can add cardiovascular strain. A less common but important possibility is takotsubo, or “broken-heart,” cardiomyopathy, in which severe stress weakens the heart’s main pumping chamber and produces symptoms resembling a heart attack, especially in women over 50. Chest tightness that is happening now, is persistent or recurrent, or comes with shortness of breath, pain spreading to the arm, back, jaw or upper abdomen, cold sweating, nausea, faintness or light-headedness should be treated as an emergency by calling 000 rather than being attributed to grief. Grief is emotional, but it is also a whole-body stress response, so sleep disruption, poor appetite, anxiety, palpitations and concentration problems can be genuine physical effects of mourning rather than “just imagination.” [shard_01169_7873] [shard_00338_37685]

Acute bereavement can increase stress hormones, heart rate, blood pressure and blood-clotting tendency, while disrupted sleep, eating and medication-taking can add cardiovascular strain. [shard_02898_63460] [shard_01169_7873]

In older adults, one study found that heart attacks or strokes occurred at twice the usual rate during the first 30 days after a partner’s death, with the excess risk then beginning to decline, so six weeks is beyond the peak period but not a reason to dismiss new symptoms. [shard_02898_63460]

A less common but important possibility is takotsubo, or “broken-heart,” cardiomyopathy, in which severe stress weakens the heart’s main pumping chamber and produces symptoms resembling a heart attack, especially in women over 50. [shard_00499_82779]

Chest tightness that is happening now, is persistent or recurrent, or comes with shortness of breath, pain spreading to the arm, back, jaw or upper abdomen, cold sweating, nausea, faintness or light-headedness should be treated as an emergency by calling 000 rather than being attributed to grief. [shard_04785_27239]

Even without those accompanying symptoms, her chest tightness warrants prompt medical assessment because anxiety can cause chest symptoms, but distinguishing anxiety from heart disease, a heart attack or takotsubo cannot safely be done at home. [shard_04785_27239] [shard_00499_82779]

Bereavement-related hormonal changes can interfere with immune regulation, and research in older bereaved people has described effects involving cortisol, T-cells, natural-killer cells and responses to influenza vaccination. [shard_03761_73428]

Inflammation may also be part of the stress response, but an association between grief and inflammatory or immune changes does not prove that grief has caused an infection, autoimmune disease, cancer or another specific illness in her. [shard_01169_7873] [shard_03761_73428]

A sensible next step is to arrange a GP appointment soon, ideally with a family member and a complete list of her medicines, missed doses, symptoms, sleep, food and fluid intake, and home blood-pressure readings if available. [shard_03006_39123]

The clinician can decide whether she needs an examination, repeated blood-pressure measurements, an ECG, blood tests, medication review or assessment for another cause of the chest, sleep, appetite or fatigue symptoms; an ECG is part of evaluating takotsubo but does not by itself make grief abnormal. [shard_00499_82779]

She should not stop, restart, double or otherwise alter blood-pressure medicines without advice about the particular drug and missed doses, because interruption of preventive medicines after bereavement has been associated with cardiovascular risk and adherence problems are common enough to deserve practical support. [shard_02898_63460]

A pharmacist or GP can help simplify the regimen, arrange refills, check affordability and interactions, and suggest a pill organiser, reminders, home monitoring or supervised medication support if she agrees. [shard_03006_39123]

Poor sleep, reduced appetite and waves of intense sadness can be normal early mourning, so the aim is not to suppress every grief symptom but to protect hydration, nutrition, medication-taking, gentle activity, sleep routine and social contact. [shard_00338_37685]

Support her by asking what would make today easier, offering meals and company, accompanying her to appointments and offering a bereavement counsellor, grief group or psychologist without insisting that she “move on” or that counselling is required for grief to be legitimate. [shard_00338_37685]

Seek a mental-health review if symptoms are persistent, worsening or interfering substantially with daily life, particularly loss of interest, hopelessness, severe withdrawal, inability to function, ongoing inability to sleep or eat, or increasing reliance on alcohol or drugs. [shard_00787_5895] [shard_05152_49859]

Any talk of wanting to die, self-harm, reckless behaviour, or inability to keep herself safe requires immediate help rather than waiting for grief to follow a timetable. [shard_05139_49258]

Do not assume that six weeks is either “too soon” for medical help or proof of depression, that every physical symptom is grief, that normal mourning cannot coexist with heart disease, or that biological stress markers would tell you how well she is grieving. [shard_02898_63460] [shard_00787_5895]
